Central Nervous System
Physiology
Stretch Reflex

The stretch reflex is a deep spinal monosynaptic reflex in which stretching a skeletal muscle causes it to contract. This lesson covers its two phases (static and dynamic), the structure and innervation of the muscle spindle, how the spindle is stimulated, the types of stretch reflex, the functions of the reflex and muscle tone, and the motor neurons of the spinal cord.

Definition and Basic Features

The stretch reflex means that stretch of a muscle leads to reflex contraction.

  • Skeletal muscle: a deep, spinal, monosynaptic reflex mediated by a center in the spinal cord.
  • Smooth muscle: myogenic in nature, i.e. it can be elicited without any connection to the CNS; there are no centers.
  • A sudden tap on a tendon stretches the muscle suddenly, stimulating the muscle spindle in its fleshy fibers and producing a visible reflex contraction (tendon jerk).
  • Smooth muscle, like skeletal muscle, has a tone that the autonomic nervous system can increase or decrease. Cardiac muscle has no tone.
  • The receptor for both phases is the muscle spindle, a deep receptor in the fleshy part of the muscle.

The two phases

Static phase (muscle tone)Dynamic phase (tendon jerk)
StimulusMaintained stretch, e.g. the pull of gravity on antigravity musclesSudden stretch, e.g. a tap on the tendon
ReceptorNuclear chain fibersNuclear bag fibers
AfferentPrimary and secondaryPrimary only
ExpressionSkeletal muscle tone: sub-tetanic, maintained, rhythmic contraction that keeps erect postureVisible reflex contraction of the whole muscle, all fibers stimulated at the same time
Muscle fiber activityAlternating activity in muscle fibersAll fibers active together

Structure of the Muscle Spindle

  • A spindle-shaped mechanoreceptor, about 4 mm long and 0.2 mm wide, surrounded by a connective tissue capsule; it is a very slowly adapting receptor.
  • It has an outer skeleton of ordinary contractile extrafusal fibers and contains 3-10 intrafusal fibers.
  • Intrafusal fibers are smaller than extrafusal fibers with unclear striations; their tapering, contractile ends connect to the sarcolemma of extrafusal fibers.
  • The central part of the intrafusal fibers is the sensory receptor area.
Nuclear bag fibersNuclear chain fibers
Number2-3 per spindle4-5 per spindle
StructureCentral part dilated like a bag with many nuclei; non-contractile centre; striated, contractile endsShorter and thinner; a row (chain) of nuclei centrally; centre lacks actin/myosin (non-contractile); contractile peripheral parts
FunctionReceptors for the dynamic stretch reflex (tendon jerk)Receptors for the static stretch reflex (muscle tone)

Innervation of the spindle

Type I (primary, annulospiral)Type II (secondary, flower spray)Alpha efferentGamma efferent
FiberThick myelinated, 16 µ, up to 100 m/sThin myelinated, 8 µ, 40 m/sAxons of large alpha cells, 14 µ, 60 m/sAxons of small gamma cells, 4 µ, 4 m/s
Ending / targetSpirals or rings around the central part of both nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibersFlower-spray endings only on nuclear chain fibersExtrafusal muscle fibersPeripheral contractile parts of intrafusal fibers: γ-d to nuclear bag, γ-s to nuclear chain

Type I and II afferents enter the cord through the dorsal roots and synapse directly with alpha cells in the anterior horn (no interneurons); efferents leave with the ventral roots.

Mode of Stimulation of the Spindle

  1. Sudden stretch of extrafusal fibers (e.g. tendon tap): stimulates nuclear bags, giving the dynamic response.
  2. Contraction of the intrafusal periphery by gamma efferent discharge (to bag via γ-d, to chain via γ-s), giving the static response. Gamma cells are stimulated by higher brain stem and cortical centers. Contraction of the peripheral parts stretches the non-contractile centre, stimulating primary (dynamic) and secondary (static) endings.
  3. Contraction of the antagonist, which stretches the muscle (e.g. biceps contraction stretches the triceps spindle).
  4. Pull of gravity, stretching mainly antigravity muscles and stimulating the static phase.

Maximal spindle stimulation occurs during passive stretch (e.g. tapping the tendon). Minimal stimulation occurs during voluntary contraction, because alpha-cell activity shortens the extrafusal fibers and releases tension on the spindle.

Types of Stretch Reflex

  • Monosynaptic: static, dynamic, and negative stretch reflexes. In the negative reflex, shortening of a muscle by its contraction leads to reflex relaxation.
  • Polysynaptic:
    • Cerebellar stretch (load) reflex: when weight is suddenly added to a flexed forearm, the forearm stays flexed. Proprioceptive impulses reach the cerebellum, which sends strong facilitatory impulses from the neocerebellum to gamma motor neurons, increasing tone and strengthening contraction.
    • Inverse stretch reflex: marked over-stretch causes reflex relaxation (inhibition) via Golgi tendon organs, protecting the muscle from rupture, through inhibitory interneurons or inhibitory cerebellar impulses on anterior horn cells.
Muscle spindleGolgi tendon organ
SiteFleshy muscle fibersTendons of muscles
StructureIntrafusal and extrafusal fibersEncapsulated network of knobby nerve endings
StimulusMuscle stretchOver-stretch
Reflex / responseStretch reflex: muscle contractionInverse stretch reflex: muscle inhibition
AfferentPrimary and secondary endingsOnly one afferent, rapidly conducting, 16 µ
ConnectionMonosynaptic, spinal cord onlyPolysynaptic, may reach the cerebellum

Functions of the Stretch Reflex

1. Muscle tone (static phase)

  • Keeps equilibrium and adjusts body posture.
  • Helps venous return and lymphatic drainage.
  • Produces heat and helps regulate body temperature.
  • Abdominal muscle tone keeps viscera in position; mastication muscle tone prevents drop of the mandible.

2. Damping (signal averaging)

Prevents skeletal muscle oscillations. Area 4 sends unequal discharges to anterior horn cells: weak impulses are made stronger in tone and strong impulses weaker, so contractions become more or less homogenous.

3. Servo-assist (α-γ co-activation)

Stretch of intrafusal fibers assists the force of extrafusal contraction without increasing discharge from higher motor areas, giving stronger contraction with minimal energy use. It is especially active when a muscle lifts a heavy weight against gravity, since the weight constantly stretches the tendon and stimulates the intrafusal fibers.

Characters of the static stretch reflex (muscle tone)

  • Deep, spinal, monosynaptic; the static phase of the stretch reflex.
  • Uses very little energy, never fatigues, and adapts very slowly.
  • Increased tone in a muscle is accompanied by inhibition in its antagonist.
  • With no interneuron in the arc: no after-discharge, no reverberating circuits, and extreme localization.

Motor Neurons of the Spinal Cord

Efferent neurons occupy mainly the anterior and lateral horns.

NeuronSupplyNotes
Large alpha cellsExtrafusal fibers of skeletal muscle70% of anterior horn cells
Gamma cellsIntrafusal fibers of skeletal muscleRelatively smaller; 30% of anterior horn cells
Lateral horn cellsOrigin of the autonomic nervous system

Key Points / Quick Review

The reflex

  • Stretch causes contraction; skeletal = deep, spinal, monosynaptic.
  • Smooth muscle: myogenic; cardiac: no tone.
  • Static phase = tone; dynamic phase = tendon jerk.

The spindle

  • 3-10 intrafusal fibers: 2-3 bag (dynamic), 4-5 chain (static).
  • Type I: bag + chain; Type II: chain only.
  • Gamma-d to bag, gamma-s to chain; alpha to extrafusal.

Stimulation

  • Sudden stretch, gamma discharge, antagonist contraction, gravity.
  • Maximal on passive stretch; minimal on voluntary contraction.

Types

  • Monosynaptic: static, dynamic, negative.
  • Polysynaptic: cerebellar (load) and inverse (Golgi tendon organ).

Functions

  • Muscle tone, damping, servo-assist (α-γ co-activation).
  • Tone: posture, venous return, heat, viscera position, mandible.

Motor neurons

  • Alpha 70%, gamma 30% of anterior horn cells.
  • Lateral horn cells: autonomic origin.
